danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Tidligt om morgenen den 6. oktober gik Pierre ud af skuret, og da han vendte tilbage, standsede han ved døren for at lege med en lille blågrå hund med en lang krop og korte, hjulbenede ben, der hoppede omkring ham. Denne lille hund boede i deres skur og sov om natten ved siden af Karatajev; den foretog sommetider udflugter ind i byen, men vendte altid tilbage. Den havde formodentlig aldrig haft en ejer, og den tilhørte stadig ingen og havde intet navn. Franskmændene kaldte den Azor; soldaten, der fortalte historier, kaldte den Femgalka; Karatajev og andre kaldte den Grå eller stundom Slasken. Dens mangel på en herre, et navn eller endda en race eller nogen bestemt farve syntes ikke at plage den blågrå hund det mindste. Dens lådne hale stod fast og rundt som en fjerbusk, dens hjulbenede poter tjente den så godt, at den ofte yndefuldt løftede et bagben og løb meget let og hurtigt på tre ben, som om den ringeagtede at bruge alle fire. Alt glædede den. Snart rullede den sig på ryggen og hvinede af fryd, snart solede den sig med en tankefuld og vigtig mine, og snart legede den muntert med en træsplint eller et strå.

Pierres påklædning bestod nu af en snavset, revet skjorte (den eneste rest af hans tidligere tøj), et par soldaterbukser, som han på Karatajevs råd bandt med snor om anklerne for varmens skyld, og en bondekappe med hue. Fysisk havde han forandret sig meget i denne tid. Han virkede ikke længere svær, skønt han stadig havde det præg af soliditet og styrke, der var arveligt i hans familie. Et skæg og overskæg dækkede den nedre del af hans ansigt, og en filtret hårtop, befængt med lus, krøllede sig rundt om hans hoved som en hue. Blikket i hans øjne var beslutsomt, roligt og livligt opmærksomt som aldrig før. Den tidligere slaphed, der selv havde vist sig i hans øjne, var nu erstattet af en energisk parathed til handling og modstand. Hans fødder var bare.

Pierre så først ned over marken, hen over hvilken køretøjer og ryttere passerede den morgen, derefter ud i det fjerne over floden, så på hunden, der lod, som om den for alvor prøvede at bide ham, og så på sine bare fødder, som han med fornøjelse anbragte i forskellige stillinger og bevægede sine snavsede, tykke storetæer. Hver gang han så på sine bare fødder, spillede et smil af livlig selvtilfredshed hen over hans ansigt. Synet af dem mindede ham om alt, hvad han havde oplevet og lært i disse uger, og den erindring var ham behagelig.
I nogle dage havde vejret været stille og klart med let frost om morgenen — hvad man kalder »indiansommer.«
I solskinnet var luften varm, og den varme var særlig behagelig med den opkvikkende friskhed fra morgenens frost stadig i luften.

Over alting — fjernt og nært — lå det magiske krystalglimt, man kun ser på den tid af efteråret. Spurvebakkerne var synlige i det fjerne med landsbyen, kirken og det store hvide hus. De nøgne træer, sandet, murstenene og tagene på husene, det grønne kirketårn og hjørnerne af det hvide hus i det fjerne — alt stod frem i den gennemsigtige luft i de fineste konturer og med en unaturlig klarhed. I nærheden kunne man se de velkendte ruiner af et halvt nedbrændt herresæde besat af franskmændene, med syrenbuskene, der stadig viste mørkegrønt ved hegnet. Og selv det ødelagte og tilsmudsede hus — der i gråvejr var frastødende grimt — virkede nu stille smukt i den klare, ubevægelige glans.
En fransk korporal med frakken knappet op på hjemlig vis, en kalot på hovedet og en kort pibe i munden kom bag hjørnet af skuret og nærmede sig Pierre med et venligt blink.
»Sikke et solskin, monsieur Kiril!« (Deres navn for Pierre.) »Hvad? Ligesom forår!«
Og korporalen lænede sig mod døren og tilbød Pierre sin pibe, skønt Pierre altid afslog, når den blev budt ham.
»At være på march i sådant vejr...« begyndte han.

Pierre spurgte, hvad der blev sagt om afmarch, og korporalen fortalte ham, at næsten alle tropper var ved at rykke ud, og at der i dag burde komme en ordre angående fangerne. Sokolov, en af soldaterne i skuret sammen med Pierre, lå for døden, og Pierre sagde til korporalen, at der burde gøres noget for ham. Korporalen svarede, at Pierre ikke behøvede at bekymre sig om det, for de havde en ambulance og et permanent hospital, og der ville blive truffet foranstaltninger for de syge, og at i det hele taget var alt, hvad der kunne ske, forudset af myndighederne.
»Desuden, monsieur Kiril, behøver De bare at sige et ord til kaptajnen, ved De. Han er en mand, der aldrig glemmer noget. Tal med kaptajnen, når han gør sin runde, han gør alt for Dem.«
(Den kaptajn, korporalen talte om, havde ofte lange samtaler med Pierre og viste ham alle slags gunstbevisninger.)

»'Ser De, Saint-Thomas,' sagde han til mig forleden dag. 'Monsieur Kiril er en dannet mand, der taler fransk. Han er en russisk herremand, der har haft uheld, men han er en mand. Han ved, hvad der er hvad... Hvis han ønsker noget og beder mig, får han ikke et afslag. Når man har studeret, ser De, så holder man af dannelse og velopdragne folk.' Det er for Deres skyld, jeg nævner det, monsieur Kiril. Forleden dag, hvis det ikke havde været for Dem, ville den sag have endt ilde.«

Og efter at have snakket lidt endnu gik korporalen sin vej. (Den sag, han havde hentydet til, var sket nogle dage forinden — et slagsmål mellem fangerne og de franske soldater, hvori Pierre havde formået at berolige sine kammerater.) Nogle af fangerne, der havde hørt Pierre tale med korporalen, spurgte straks, hvad franskmanden havde sagt. Mens Pierre gentog, hvad han havde fået at vide om hærens afmarch fra Moskva, kom en tynd, gustengul, pjaltet fransk soldat hen til skurets dør. Hurtigt og sky løftede han fingrene til panden til hilsen og spurgte Pierre, om soldaten Platoche, som han havde givet en skjorte til syning, var i det skur.
En uge forinden var de franske soldater blevet forsynet med støvlelæder og lærred, som de havde givet til fangerne for at lave støvler og skjorter af.
»Færdig, færdig, min gode mand!« sagde Karatajev og kom ud med en pænt sammenfoldet skjorte.

Karatajev var på grund af det varme vejr og for nemheds skyld ved arbejdet kun iført bukser og en fillede skjorte, sort som sod. Hans hår var bundet rundt, på håndværkervis, med en strimmel lindetræsbast, og hans runde ansigt virkede rundere og mere elskværdigt end nogensinde.
»Et løfte er et løftes broder! Jeg sagde fredag, og her er den, færdig,« sagde Platón med et smil og foldede den skjorte ud, han havde syet.

Franskmanden så sig uroligt omkring og lod derpå, som om han overvandt sin tøven, hurtigt sin uniform falde og trak skjorten på. Han havde en lang, fedtet, blomstret silkevest nærmest sin gustne, tynde bare krop, men ingen skjorte. Han var åbenbart bange for, at fangerne, der så på, ville le ad ham, og stak hastigt hovedet ind i skjorten. Ingen af fangerne sagde et ord.
»Se, den sidder godt!« blev Platón ved med at gentage, idet han glattede skjorten.
Franskmanden stak hovedet og hænderne igennem og så uden at løfte øjnene ned på skjorten og undersøgte sømmene.

»Ser du, min gode mand, dette er ikke et systue, og jeg havde ikke ordentligt værktøj; og som man siger, der skal et værktøj til selv for at slå en lus ihjel,« sagde Platón med et af sine runde smil, tydeligt tilfreds med sit arbejde.
»Det er godt, ganske godt, tak,« sagde franskmanden på fransk, »men der må være noget lærred tilovers.«
»Den kommer til at sidde endnu bedre, når den har lagt sig til kroppen,« sagde Karatajev, stadig beundrende sit håndværk. »Så bliver det dejlig og behageligt...«

»Tak, tak, gamle ven... Men stumperne, der er tilovers?« sagde franskmanden igen og smilede. Han tog en assignationsrubelseddel frem og gav den til Karatajev. »Men giv mig de stykker, der er tilovers.«

Pierre så, at Platón ikke ville forstå, hvad franskmanden sagde, og han så til uden at blande sig. Karatajev takkede franskmanden for pengene og blev ved med at beundre sit eget arbejde. Franskmanden insisterede på at få de tiloversbleven stykker tilbage og bad Pierre om at oversætte.
»Hvad skal han med stumperne?« sagde Karatajev. »De ville blive fine benviklere for os. Nå, det er vel lige meget.«

Og Karatajev tog med et pludselig forandret og bedrøvet udtryk en lille bundt affaldsstykker frem inde fra sin skjorte og gav den til franskmanden uden at se på ham. »Åh, du milde!« mumlede Karatajev og gik sin vej. Franskmanden betragtede lærredet, betænkte sig et øjeblik, så derpå spørgende på Pierre, og som om Pierres blik havde sagt ham noget, rødmede han pludselig og råbte med en hvinende stemme:
»Platoche! Hør, Platoche! Behold dem selv!« Og han rakte stumperne tilbage, vendte sig om og gik.

»Der kan du bare se,« sagde Karatajev og vippede med hovedet. »Folk sagde, de var ikke kristne, men de har også sjæle. Det er, som de gamle plejede at sige: 'En svedende hånd er en åben hånd, en tør hånd er en nærrig hånd.' Han er nøgen, men alligevel gav han dem tilbage.«
Karatajev smilede tankefuldt og var tavs et stykke tid, mens han betragtede stumperne.
»Men de bliver til pragtfulde benviklere, kære ven,« sagde han og gik ind i skuret igen.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: Early in the morning of October sixth, Pierre went out of the shed and, on his way back, stopped by the door to play with a little blue-gray dog with a long body and short, bowed legs that was jumping around him. This little dog lived in their shed, sleeping beside Karataev at night. It sometimes wandered into town but always came back. It had probably never had an owner—it belonged to nobody and had no name. The French called it Azor; the soldier who told stories called it Femgalka; Karataev and the others called it Gray, or sometimes Flabby. Having no master, no name, and not even a definite breed or color didn't seem to bother the blue-gray dog in the least. Its furry tail stood up firm and round like a plume, its crooked little legs served it so well that it would often gracefully lift a hind leg and trot along quickly on three legs, as if disdaining to use all four. Everything pleased it. One moment it would roll on its back yelping with delight, the next it would bask in the sun with an air of self-important thoughtfulness, then frolic around playing with a stick or a piece of straw.

Pierre's outfit now consisted of a dirty, torn shirt (the only remnant of his former clothing), a pair of soldier's trousers that he tied at the ankles with string on Karataev's advice for warmth, and a peasant coat and cap. He had changed a great deal physically. He no longer looked stout, though he still had the solid, strong build that ran in his family. A beard and mustache covered the lower part of his face, and a tangle of hair, infested with lice, curled around his head like a cap. The look in his eyes was resolute, calm, and alertly alive—unlike anything before. The old slackness that had shown even in his eyes was now replaced by an energetic readiness for action and resistance. His feet were bare.

Pierre first looked across the field where vehicles and riders were passing that morning, then into the distance across the river, then at the dog pretending to seriously bite him, and then down at his own bare feet, which he placed in various positions with obvious pleasure, wiggling his dirty, thick big toes. Every time he looked at his bare feet, a smile of amused self-satisfaction crossed his face. The sight of them reminded him of everything he had experienced and learned during these weeks, and the memory was pleasant.
For several days the weather had been calm and clear, with slight frosts in the morning—what people call an 'old wives' summer.'
In the sunshine the air was warm, and that warmth was especially pleasant alongside the invigorating freshness of the morning frost still lingering in the air.

On everything near and far lay that magical crystal shimmer you see only in autumn. The Sparrow Hills were visible in the distance—the village, the church, the large white house. The bare trees, the sand, the bricks and rooftops, the green church spire, and the corners of the white house all stood out in the transparent air with an unnaturally delicate clarity. Nearby were the familiar ruins of a half-burned mansion occupied by the French, with lilac bushes still showing dark green beside the fence. Even that ruined, defiled house—repulsively ugly in dull weather—looked quietly beautiful now in the clear, motionless light.
A French corporal, his coat unbuttoned in a homey way, a skullcap on his head and a short pipe in his mouth, came around the corner of the shed and approached Pierre with a friendly wink.
'What sunshine, Monsieur Kiril!' (That was their name for Pierre.) 'Just like spring!'
And the corporal leaned against the door and offered Pierre his pipe, though Pierre always declined it.
'To be on the march in such weather...' he began.

Pierre asked what was being said about leaving, and the corporal told him that nearly all the troops were departing and there should be orders about the prisoners that day. Sokolov, one of the soldiers sharing Pierre's shed, was dying, and Pierre told the corporal that something should be done about him. The corporal replied that Pierre needn't worry—they had an ambulance and a hospital, and arrangements would be made for the sick. In general, everything that could happen had been anticipated by the authorities.

'Besides, Monsieur Kiril, you only have to say a word to the captain, you know. He's a man who never forgets anything. Have a word with the captain when he makes his rounds—he'll do anything for you.'
(The captain the corporal mentioned often had long conversations with Pierre and showed him all kinds of favors.)

'"You see, St. Thomas," he said to me the other day, "Monsieur Kiril is an educated man who speaks French. He's a Russian gentleman who's had bad luck, but he's a real man. He knows what's what. If he needs anything and asks me, he won't be refused. When a man has had an education, you see, he appreciates learning and well-bred people." I mention this for your sake, Monsieur Kiril. The other day, if it hadn't been for you, that business would have ended badly.'

After chatting a while longer, the corporal went away. (The incident he'd mentioned had happened a few days earlier—a fight between the prisoners and the French soldiers, in which Pierre had managed to calm his comrades down.) Some prisoners who had overheard Pierre talking to the corporal immediately asked what the Frenchman had said. While Pierre was relaying the news about the army leaving Moscow, a thin, sallow, ragged French soldier came to the shed door. Quickly and timidly raising his fingers to his forehead in greeting, he asked Pierre whether the soldier Platoche—to whom he had given a shirt to sew—was in this shed.
A week earlier, the French had been issued boot leather and linen, which they'd given to the prisoners to make into boots and shirts.
'Ready, ready, my friend!' said Karataev, coming out with a neatly folded shirt.

Karataev, because of the warm weather and for ease of work, was wearing only trousers and a tattered shirt as black as soot. His hair was tied up workman-style with a strip of lime bark, and his round face looked rounder and more pleasant than ever.
'A promise is a sacred thing! I said Friday, and here it is—ready,' said Platon, smiling as he unfolded the shirt he had sewn.

The Frenchman glanced around nervously, then, as if overcoming his hesitation, quickly pulled off his uniform and put on the shirt. Under the uniform, next to his sallow, thin bare body, he wore a long, greasy, flowered silk waistcoat—but no shirt. He was clearly afraid the watching prisoners would laugh at him, and thrust his head into the shirt quickly. None of the prisoners said a word.
'See, it fits nicely!' Platon kept saying, smoothing the shirt straight.
The Frenchman pushed his head and hands through without looking up, examining the shirt and checking the seams.

'You know, my friend, this isn't a tailor's shop, and I didn't have the right tools. As they say, you need the proper tool even to crack a louse,' said Platon with one of his warm, round smiles, clearly pleased with his work.
'It's good, quite good, thank you,' said the Frenchman in French, 'but there must be some fabric left over.'
'It'll fit even better once it settles to your body,' said Karataev, still admiring his handiwork. 'You'll be nice and comfortable...'
'Thanks, thanks, old fellow... But the leftover pieces?' the Frenchman said again, smiling. He took out a ruble note and gave it to Karataev. 'But give me the scraps that are left.'

Pierre saw that Platon didn't want to understand what the Frenchman was saying, and he watched without interfering. Karataev thanked the Frenchman for the money and went on admiring his own work. The Frenchman insisted on getting back the leftover material and asked Pierre to translate.
'What does he want the scraps for?' said Karataev. 'They'd make fine leg wrappings for us. Well, never mind.'

And Karataev, his face suddenly changed and saddened, took a small bundle of scraps from inside his shirt and handed it to the Frenchman without looking at him. 'Oh well!' he muttered, and walked away. The Frenchman looked at the cloth, thought for a moment, then glanced inquiringly at Pierre and—as if Pierre's expression told him something—suddenly blushed and shouted in a squeaky voice:
'Platoche! Hey, Platoche! Keep them yourself!' And handing back the scraps, he turned and walked out.

'There, look at that,' said Karataev, shaking his head. 'People said they weren't Christians, but they have souls too. It's what the old folks used to say: "A sweating hand is an open hand, a dry hand is a tight one." He's got nothing himself, but he gave them back.'
Karataev smiled thoughtfully and sat quietly for a while, looking at the pieces of cloth.
'But they'll make wonderful leg wrappings, my friend,' he said, and went back into the shed.
